title: The AI Budget Is Growing. Is the Contact Center Getting Better?
summary: AI spending in contact centers is accelerating, but are operations actually improving? Explore how to measure AI's impact on customer outcomes, productivity, quality, and business performance.
body_markdown:
AI has moved from an experimental line item to a major component of contact center budgets. Organizations are investing in chatbots, voicebots, agent assist, automated quality assurance, conversation intelligence, and increasingly sophisticated AI platforms designed to automate entire workflows.


The spending is significant. According to[Gartner research published in August 2026](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-08-26-gartner-survey-finds-ai-spending-by-customer-service-leaders-has-surged-by-38-percent-despite-overall-service-and-support-function-budgets-rising-by-just-2-percent) , AI spending among surveyed customer service leaders increased 38%, while overall service and support budgets grew just 2%. That suggests organizations are making deliberate tradeoffs, redirecting resources toward technology even as broader budgets remain constrained.


But there's another finding worth considering. In[separate Gartner research](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-07-08-gartner-survey-finds-customers-are-three-times-more-likely-to-use-third-party-genai-than-company-provided-chatbots-for-customer-service?trk=public_post_comment-text) , only 24% of surveyed service and support leaders demonstrated positive financial returns across their AI use cases.


The industry clearly believes AI will transform customer service. The harder question is whether organizations can demonstrate that the transformation is actually happening.


## Buying AI and Improving Operations Are Two Different Things


There's a predictable pattern when organizations introduce new technology.


First comes the business case. Leaders identify an opportunity, estimate potential savings, evaluate vendors, and secure funding. Then comes implementation, followed by training, adoption, and the inevitable pressure to show results.


Somewhere along the way, it's easy for the definition of success to shift.


Instead of asking whether the operation is performing better, organizations begin reporting how many employees are using the technology, how many conversations AI has analyzed, how many customer interactions a chatbot has handled, or how many hours a tool claims to have saved.


Those numbers can be useful. They tell you whether technology is being used and whether it is performing its intended activities.


But they don't necessarily tell you whether the investment is delivering the business outcome you expected.


**AI activity is not the same thing as operational improvement.**


## Productivity Is Valuable. But Where Does the Value Go?


Consider a contact center that introduces AI-generated call summaries.


Before implementation, agents spend two minutes completing after-call notes. With AI, that work takes 30 seconds. Across thousands of calls, the potential time savings are substantial.


That's a meaningful productivity improvement. But what happens to the time?


If agents handle more interactions without sacrificing quality, the organization may gain capacity. If the time allows agents to focus on more complicated customer needs, the experience may improve. If it reduces overtime or enables the organization to manage growth without proportional hiring, there may be a measurable financial benefit.


But if the time simply disappears into existing workflows without changing capacity, cost, quality, or employee experience, the operational return may be harder to demonstrate.


The same question applies to automated QA. Evaluating 100% of conversations instead of a small sample creates much broader visibility, but the value depends on what the organization does with that information. Does it identify compliance risks earlier? Improve coaching? Reduce repeat contacts? Help supervisors intervene before problems become widespread?


**Productivity creates an opportunity for value. It doesn't automatically capture that value.**


## A Successful Automation Can Still Produce a Bad Customer Experience


Customer-facing AI introduces another measurement challenge.


Imagine a company deploys a chatbot and successfully reduces the number of conversations reaching human agents. From an operational perspective, the results may initially look promising. Automation rates increase, assisted contact volume declines, and the cost of handling routine questions appears to fall.


But what if customers are struggling to complete their tasks? What if they have to contact the company multiple times? What if the chatbot provides an answer but cannot actually resolve the issue?


The organization may have reduced human involvement without reducing customer effort.


This distinction matters because automation and resolution are not interchangeable. A conversation can end without the customer's problem being solved, just as a customer can abandon a digital interaction and return through another channel.


Organizations need to understand not only how much work AI handles, but whether customers are getting what they came for.


That means examining outcomes such as successful resolution, repeat contacts, escalation patterns, customer effort, and the quality of transitions between AI and human agents.


A high automation rate is only a success if the experience works.


## The Human Operation Should Be Getting Better, Too


Not every AI investment is designed to replace work. Some of the most valuable applications are intended to help people perform better.


Real-time agent assist can help employees find information, navigate unfamiliar situations, and respond more consistently. Conversation intelligence can help supervisors identify emerging issues. Automated QA can expand performance visibility beyond a handful of sampled calls.


But those capabilities should produce observable changes in the operation.


Are new agents becoming proficient faster? Are supervisors spending less time searching for coaching opportunities and more time coaching? Are compliance issues being identified earlier? Are agents resolving complicated situations more effectively? Are customers getting clearer, more consistent answers?


These are different measures from adoption or usage, and they often require looking across several operational systems.


An agent may use AI guidance regularly without becoming more effective. A supervisor may have access to significantly more performance data without making better decisions. A QA program may evaluate every conversation without improving quality.


The technology creates the capability. The organization still has to turn that capability into results.


## More Technology Can Also Mean More Complexity


There's another cost that doesn't always receive enough attention in AI business cases: the operational complexity introduced by the technology itself.


A contact center may now have separate tools for transcription, automated QA, agent assist, knowledge management, analytics, summarization, and customer-facing automation. Each system may require configuration, integration, administration, training, and ongoing oversight.


Individually, each investment may solve a legitimate problem. Collectively, they can create new work.


Supervisors may need to navigate multiple dashboards to understand performance. Agents may receive guidance from one system while searching for information in another. Operations teams may spend time reconciling inconsistent reporting. IT teams may inherit additional integration and maintenance responsibilities.


This doesn't mean organizations should avoid specialized technology. It means the value of a new capability should be considered alongside the effort required to operate it.


If AI eliminates five minutes of manual work but introduces five minutes of investigation, administration, or coordination somewhere else, the organization may not be as far ahead as it thinks.


**The goal should be a simpler, more effective operation, not simply a more technologically sophisticated one.**


## The Economics Are Different for BPOs


For BPOs, measuring the impact of AI can be even more complicated because operational improvements don't always translate directly into commercial value.


Consider a BPO that uses AI to reduce average handle time or automate a portion of its QA process. The operational benefit may be clear, but who captures the financial value depends on the commercial arrangement.


Under some pricing models, efficiency gains improve the BPO's margins. Under others, reduced handling time or contact volume may lower billable revenue. Clients may expect savings to be passed through, while the BPO still bears the cost of technology, implementation, and ongoing management.


That creates an important strategic question: is AI simply making the existing service cheaper, or is it making the BPO more valuable to its clients?


The latter creates a broader opportunity. A BPO that can demonstrate stronger compliance, better customer outcomes, faster identification of emerging issues, and more actionable customer intelligence may have a more compelling commercial proposition than one that competes primarily on labor efficiency.


For BPO leaders, the AI investment conversation needs to include client retention, differentiation, service quality, and the ability to offer capabilities clients couldn't easily obtain before.


Otherwise, the organization risks investing heavily in technology while continuing to compete on the same economics.


## Start With the Outcome, Then Work Backward


One practical way to improve accountability is to define the operational change an AI investment is supposed to produce before deciding how to measure success.


Different investments should have different success criteria.


-


**Customer-facing automation:** Are customers resolving their issues successfully, with less effort and fewer repeat contacts?


-


**Agent assist:** Are agents becoming more effective, accurate, and confident when handling complex interactions?


-


**Automated QA:** Are quality issues being identified earlier, coaching becoming more targeted, and performance improving?


-


**Conversation intelligence:** Are leaders discovering and resolving operational problems faster?


-


**AI-generated summaries:** Is administrative work declining, and is that time translating into measurable capacity or service improvements?


These measures should be established against a baseline, then evaluated over time. Where possible, organizations should compare similar groups or workflows and account for changes in contact volume, customer mix, and complexity.


It's also worth distinguishing between leading indicators and business outcomes. Better guidance usage or faster issue detection may signal progress, but leaders should continue following the chain to see whether those improvements affect quality, efficiency, risk, or customer experience.


The question isn't simply whether the tool works.


It's whether the business works better because the tool exists.


## AI Needs an Operational Owner, Not Just a Technology Owner


One reason AI investments can struggle to demonstrate value is that responsibility becomes fragmented.


IT owns implementation. A vendor owns the technology. Operations owns performance. QA owns evaluation. Training owns employee readiness. Finance wants to understand the return.


Everyone owns part of the investment, but no one may own the complete outcome.


That creates a gap between deploying a capability and ensuring that the organization actually benefits from it.


If conversation intelligence identifies a recurring customer problem, who is responsible for investigating it? If automated QA reveals that agents consistently struggle with a particular behavior, who updates coaching? If AI guidance isn't improving performance, who determines whether the problem is content, adoption, configuration, or the underlying process?


At MosaicVoice, we see the greatest potential when conversation intelligence, automated QA, coaching, and real-time guidance are connected to the decisions and actions that follow. An insight is useful because someone can act on it, measure what changes, and continue improving.


Technology shouldn't simply generate more information about the operation. It should help the operation respond.


## The Next Phase of AI Investment Is Accountability


The first wave of AI adoption was largely about possibility. Organizations wanted to understand what the technology could do, where it could be deployed, and how quickly they could introduce it.


The next phase requires a different discipline.


Leaders need to know which investments are producing measurable improvements, which are creating promising but unrealized opportunities, and which may not be delivering enough value to justify their cost.


That may mean expanding a successful use case, redesigning an underperforming workflow, consolidating overlapping tools, or discontinuing something that isn't producing the expected results.


It also means being willing to recognize benefits that don't fit neatly into a labor-savings calculation. Better compliance, improved customer retention, stronger employee performance, and faster operational decisions can create substantial value, even when they don't immediately reduce headcount.


The important thing is to define that value, measure it credibly, and connect it to business priorities.


## The Bottom Line


AI spending in customer service is growing quickly, and there are good reasons for that investment. The technology can automate repetitive work, improve access to information, expand quality monitoring, and reveal insights that were previously difficult to uncover.


But none of those capabilities guarantees a better contact center.


The real measure of success is whether customers get better outcomes, employees become more effective, operations become more efficient, risks are managed more consistently, and the business becomes stronger.


That requires looking beyond deployments, usage statistics, and estimated time savings to understand what has actually changed.


The AI budget is growing.


**The contact center should have something meaningful to show for it.**
